scenes.tts: The kidney's aldosterone receptor binds cortisol just as tightly as it binds aldosterone. Adult human plasma carries far more cortisol than aldosterone. A hundredfold molar excess is a commonly cited figure. Yet sodium transport in the kidney follows aldosterone. How? The answer is an enzyme beside the receptor.
scenes.visual: receptor with two steroids that both fit; a crowd of cortisol against one aldosterone; a question-mark box beside the receptor
scenes.narration: The kidney's aldosterone receptor binds cortisol just as tightly as it binds aldosterone. Adult human plasma carries far more cortisol than aldosterone. A hundredfold molar excess is a commonly cited figure. Yet sodium transport in the kidney follows aldosterone. How? The answer is an enzyme beside the receptor.

scenes.tts: In nineteen sixty-one, Jean Crabbé used a toad's urinary bladder, which moves sodium from urine side to blood side. He cut each bladder into paired halves and gave aldosterone to one half. After about one hour, its short-circuit current rose above its partner's. Tracer fluxes in eight bladders showed that the extra current was net sodium transport. So in this preparation, aldosterone acts on the epithelium directly.
scenes.visual: two paired chambers with a sheet between; aldosterone added to one half; its current gauge rises after about one hour

scenes.tts: Now the puzzle. In extracts of kidney and other tissues, mineralocorticoid receptors bound aldosterone and the physiological glucocorticoids with equal affinity. In humans, that glucocorticoid is cortisol, and it circulates at far higher concentrations. On those numbers, cortisol should occupy the receptor nearly all the time. So selectivity is not in the receptor.
scenes.visual: both steroids dock equally; cortisol crowd fills the socket and aldosterone waits

scenes.tts: The answer came in nineteen eighty-eight. John Funder and colleagues reported that targets such as kidney, colon and parotid carry an enzyme, eleven beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase. It converts cortisol to inactive cortisone. Aldosterone escapes this conversion. So the enzyme lowers cortisol near the receptor, and the receptor is left to aldosterone. Edwards and colleagues in Edinburgh reached a similar conclusion the same year.
scenes.visual: the question-mark box becomes the enzyme; cortisol turns to grey cortisone at it; aldosterone passes and docks

scenes.tts: Liquorice fits this idea. Eating large amounts of liquorice was long known to cause sodium retention, low potassium and high blood pressure. Renin and aldosterone are both low. That looks like mineralocorticoid excess without the mineralocorticoid. Glycyrrhetinic acid in liquorice inhibits the enzyme, so cortisol is no longer inactivated in the kidney. It occupies the mineralocorticoid receptor itself.

scenes.tts: The conclusion has limits. It came from work on rats and corticosterone. The epithelial type two form of the enzyme was characterized in the nineteen nineties. Keep this rule. The enzyme beside a receptor is part of what defines a hormone's target tissue.
